extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of American Civil War / naval history
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of naval operations, ship design, logistics, and joint (army‑navy) strategy in the American Civil War, with emphasis on 1862 campaigns such as Hampton Roads and New Orleans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea-power as decisive strategic factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Sea-power kept the North in affluence while it starved the South. Sea-power...gradually cut them off from the whole world's base of war supplies, a force which enabled the Union armies to get and keep the strangle‑hold which did the South to death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess naval control by its effects on supply lines, economic resources, and the ability to project power ashore; a navy that isolates an enemy's external bases and sustains its own armies is strategically decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blockade effectiveness and persistent vigilance
rubrics_metrics.description: The blockade declared in April was no empty threat... Three thousand miles of Southern coastline was, however, more than the North could blockade or even watch to its own satisfaction... Fogs, storms, and clever ruses played their part on behalf of those who ran the blockade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate blockade success by coverage of coastline, interdiction of contraband, and ability to cope with weather, deception, and blockade‑runners; recognize the human cost of long monotony and the need for sustained resources and vigilance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial and engineering resources determine naval superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Owing to the vastly superior resources of the North in marine engineering, armor‑plating, and all other points of naval construction... the Monitor enjoyed enormous advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a side's advantage by its shipbuilding capacity, access to armor/engines, and technical expertise; industrial superiority can offset numerical parity or unconventional enemy designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ship design trade‑offs: draft, maneuverability, armor, armament
rubrics_metrics.description: The Monitor was small, light‑draught, maneuverable, turreted, and carried two powerful eleven‑inch guns; the Merrimac had heavy draught, four‑inch plating, ten guns, poor engines, and was unwieldy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing warships, balance draft (for shallows), maneuverability, protection, firepower, and engine reliability; consider operational environment (coastal, riverine, open sea) and crew competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crew quality and training matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Her whole crew numbered only 58; but every single one was a trained professional naval seaman... the crew [of the Merrimac] were mostly landsmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess combat effectiveness not only by hardware but by the degree of professional training and experience of crews; well‑trained small crews can outperform larger untrained complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capturing and holding strategic coastal bases
rubrics_metrics.description: The capture of Hatteras Island... Ship Island... Port Royal... New Orleans was a most pregnant Federal victory; for it established a Union base at the great strategic point where sea‑power and land‑power could meet most effectively in Mississippi waters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate operations for their ability to secure bases that link sea and land operations; success is measured by the extent to which bases enable blockade tightening, supply, and further penetration inland.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of combined (navy + army) operations to seize and hold territory
rubrics_metrics.description: Amphibious forces—fleets and armies combined—were essential. There was no use in parading up and down the river... An army to seize and hold strategic points ashore was absolutely indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge campaigns by the degree of effective joint planning and execution; navies can take positions but armies are required to hold and exploit them—lack of cooperation produces ephemeral gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistics and lines of communication are critical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The long, precarious line of communications... 'I arrived in New Orleans with five or six days' provisions and one anchor... Fighting is nothing to the evils of the river—getting on shore, running foul of one another, losing anchors, etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate operational plans against sustainment realities: provisioning, spare equipment (anchors), secure supply routes, and the risk of ships being stranded or isolated; logistical shortfalls can negate tactical victories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed defenses vs. mobile forces: strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The forts were strong... But they suffered from all the disadvantages of fixed defenses opposed by a mobile enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing defenses, account for the mobility and reach of the attacker; strong static fortifications can be bypassed or isolated if the attacker controls sea/river approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riverine navigation hazards and engineering obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: The boom across the river... the four‑knot spring current was so strong that the eight‑knot ships could not make way enough against it... the configuration of the channel... shoaling of the water... the difficulties of the passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan operations with detailed appreciation of currents, channels, obstructions (booms, chained vessels), tides, and shoals; engineering solutions and local piloting are mission‑critical for river operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper task organization and asset employment
rubrics_metrics.description: A weak point, however, was the presence of mortar‑boats that would have been better out of the way altogether... The Government wished to cut off the branches first; while Farragut wished to cut down the tree itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate force composition and the placement of specialized assets against the commander’s operational concept; misapplied assets (e.g., mortar‑boats in Farragut's plan) can hinder rather than help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical formation and lead-ship selection matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The passage was made... in line‑ahead (that is, one after another) because Farragut found the opening narrower than he thought it should be for two columns abreast... The leading vessel, drawing most fire, should have been the strongest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tactical arrangements—formation, sequencing, and which ship leads—by exposure to enemy fire and ability to absorb damage; avoid placing weaker vessels in the most vulnerable lead positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiative and judgement of commanders versus rigid orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Farragut's own infinitely better plan was to run past the forts and take New Orleans first... he followed a course in which anything short of complete success would mean the ruin of his whole career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the value of local initiative based on operational understanding; commanders who adapt instructions to circumstances may achieve decisive results when central directives are ill‑suited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of overextension and impracticable strategic orders
rubrics_metrics.description: He therefore felt bound to obey and do all that could be done to carry on a quite impossible campaign... His big ships would certainly be stranded if he went up and waited for the army to come down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate orders for feasibility given terrain, force composition, and support; recognize when strategic directives risk overextension and potential catastrophic losses if prerequisites (e.g., army support) are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval expansion strains personnel and command structures
rubrics_metrics.description: During this year the number of vessels in commission grew from 264 to 427. Yet such a form of expansion was much simpler than that of the enlisted men; and the expansion of even the most highly trained enlisted personnel was very much simpler than the corresponding expansion of the officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing rapid fleet growth, include personnel recruitment, training pipelines, and officer cadre development; material increases without proportional skilled personnel degrade effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oversea patrols and legal/diplomatic constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: This oversea patrol was the most effective, because it went straight to the source of trouble. But it required extraordinary vigilance, because it had to be conducted from beyond the three‑mile limit, and with the greatest care for all the rights of neutrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure maritime interdiction efforts against international law and neutral rights; effective overseas operations must balance interdiction with diplomatic/legal constraints to avoid incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce protection is resource‑intensive and often less effective than blockade
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce protection on the high seas was an exceedingly harassing affair... The Union navy lacked the means of patrolling the sea lanes of commerce over millions... Consequently the war‑risk insurance rose... The incessant calls for recruits... robbed the merchant service of its men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize missions by cost‑benefit: protecting trade across vast sea lanes may be impossible; concentrated blockade and overseas patrols targeting contraband sources can be more effective than broad commerce protection.
